Single Pleated Filter Initial bench-scale parametric testing was performed using one pleated filter. The relative humidity (RH) during the adsorption step varied between 50% and 70% due to cycle-to-cycle variations in the air inlet temperature. During desorption, dried and compressed outdoor air flowed through a water tank at room temperature, generating humidity at about 80% RH. Over the course of 70 cycles, a range of air flow rates and regeneration temperatures were investigated to optimize the amount of CO captured and desorbed. 2 The range of conditions is summarized in Table 5. Cumulative CO adsorbed and desorbed during cycles on a single pleated filter in the bench unit. 2 Figure 13 shows the cumulative CO that was adsorbed and desorbed in each cycle, with notations of the 2 conditions that were varied over the course of the test. The fluctuation of the adsorption/desorption capacity was attributed to the variation in ambient temperature and RH over time. There was no significant effect of air flow rate on overall working capacity observed when the duration of the adsorption step was held constant while varying air feed flow rates. However, adsorption rate does increase with space velocity as expected. As shown by the breakthrough curves in Figure 14, the outlet gas reaches nearly full CO 2 breakthrough prior to the completion of the 45-minute adsorption duration, indicating higher apparent adsorption rates at higher space velocities. DE-FE0032254 The regeneration temperature was increased from 75°C to 85°C in 5 °C intervals over the course of the cycles (Figure 15). A corresponding increase in working capacity was observed when raising the regeneration temperature from 70°C to 75°C. A further increase in the temperature did not affect working capacity, indicating that higher temperature has minimal benefit to the overall productivity of the system under the conditions tested. However, regeneration temperature did impact the CO concentration in the 2 product gas. As shown in Figure 15, the peak CO concentration is higher at 80°C and 85°C, which may 2 be owed to faster desorption kinetics at these temperatures. Figure 15.
